what: LKQ is the largest distributor of alternative and recycled vehicle replacement parts. It supplies repair shops and insurers with salvage parts recovered from wrecked cars, aftermarket parts made by third parties and remanufactured components, in North America and across Europe.
customers: Collision and mechanical repair shops, insurers that steer repair work to cheaper parts, and car dealerships, plus specialty customers for recreational vehicle and performance parts.
money: Recycled and aftermarket collision and mechanical parts for repair shops.
Mechanical parts distribution to independent garages across Western and Central Europe.
RV and performance parts, and self-service salvage yards.
moat: Its network of salvage yards and distribution centres gives it the widest parts availability and fastest delivery, and insurers favour it because recycled and aftermarket parts cut claim costs.
risks: European demand is weak, and that segment is now its biggest.
Electric vehicles need fewer replacement mechanical parts over time.
Fewer accident claims, as insurance costs rise and drivers file fewer claims, hit collision part volumes.
opportunities: Rising repair costs push insurers toward cheaper alternative parts, which is exactly what LKQ sells.
Portfolio simplification and cost cuts could lift margins from a low base.
watch: Organic parts revenue per day in North America and Europe. Revenue has been flat for five years at about $13.5 billion, so organic growth is the number that shows whether the business is turning.
view: LKQ trades at about 5.4 times EV/EBITDA, 7.7 times free cash flow and 0.35 times sales, which is the valuation of a business the market thinks is in slow decline. Revenue has indeed gone nowhere - $13.1 billion in 2021, about $13.5 billion now - and the European business, which it built through acquisitions, has struggled with a weak economy and integration costs. The reported P/E of about 18 is inflated by restructuring charges; on cash flow the shares look cheap.

The core North American business is better than the headline numbers suggest. Insurers want to pay less for repairs, and an aftermarket or recycled bumper costs much less than a carmaker’s part. That makes LKQ a natural partner to the insurers who direct a large share of collision repair work. The long-term threat everyone cites is electric vehicles needing fewer parts, but collision repair does not change with the drivetrain, and EV repairs are, if anything, more expensive.

What the whole thing turns on is Europe and management’s willingness to simplify. A smaller, more focused company with a well-run North American core could deserve a far higher multiple than this. Until the European business stabilises, the stock will stay a value trap in the eyes of many investors, and I would treat it as a cheap, cash-generative holding where the catalyst has to come from management rather than the market.
bull: Europe stabilises, portfolio pruning sharpens the focus, and the shares re-rate toward a normal multiple on strong free cash flow.
bear: Collision claims keep falling, Europe stays weak, and flat revenue turns into a slow decline that justifies the low valuation.
